It's an interesting movie, if you can get over its similarities to The Wicker Man which is greatly superior on every level. A group of grad students go to a northern location in Sweden to take part in an ancient pagan 9-day festival that is held only once every 90 years. As the festival progresses, the friendly Swedes begin to reveal themselves as not quite so harmless and nice as they first appeared to be. The students begin to disappear one by one, and it finally dawns on the last survivors that none of them are ever going to make it out of the village.

I found the pace of this movie to be about the same as that of the Greenland ice sheet. I don't mind slow movies but this was a bit much even for me. Rituals, folk dances, costumes, rune designs, were all plausible, although I did notice that one of the runes, which were supposed to be from the Elder Futhark, was not a rune in the Elder Futhark, but was an English rune. Oh well, probably most people will not notice. The mythological trappings were harvested from a grab bag of different cultures. Mostly there was a mixture of Nordic and Celtic traditions. A lot of it was just invented from nothing, and had no historical source. For example, the temple in the shape of a pyramid in which the sacrifices were burned -- the pyramid had no use or significance to the pagan Swedes. Pyramids were big in Egypt, Mesopotamia and the Americas, not in Sweden.

The acting was good, but the characters were a bit lifeless and their responses to situations were not realisitic or believable. The conversion of the central character, an hysterical young woman on medications, to the pagan beliefs of the village, seemed unnatural and unlikely. She decides to watch her lover tortured and burned to death because he had sex with another women. Yeah, I know women can be bitchy, but this response seemed a bit harsh, particularly since her boyfriend was drugged out of his mind at the time by the pagans.

This movie suffers from vagueness. There is no strong central character -- no Lord Summerisle -- to tie it together and give it momentum. The writer had no real story to tell. The grad students go to the village for a holiday, and gradually they are killed as sacrifices until the last woman decides she wants to join them. Where's the story? Where are the twists and turns, the surprises, the interactions, the revelations? I mean, they are there, but they are pale and bloodless ... except for the part where a large wooden mallet is used to bash in the skulls of two old people -- lots of blood in that scene.

I would advise you to watch this movie if you are a fan of the occult, mythology, paganism, New Age beliefs. If not, you will probably find it boring and wonder why you wasted your time.
